questions: What kind of task do you find easiest to concentrate on?
Where do you usually go when you really need to focus on something?
Do you concentrate better with background noise or in complete silence? Why do you think that is?
Was it easier for you to focus a few years ago than it is now?
Is there anything you've tried recently to improve your concentration?
Which app on your phone do you open most often?
Is there an app you use for something surprising — something it probably wasn't designed for?
Have you ever deleted an app because it was taking up too much of your time?
Do you use different apps now from the ones you used two or three years ago?
If you could only keep three apps on your phone, which would survive?

part2.title: Describe a memorable conversation you had with a stranger.
bullets: who this person was and where you met them
part2.explain: and explain why this conversation has stayed with you, and whether it changed how you feel about talking to people you don't know.
followups: Did you stay in contact with this person afterwards?
Do you usually start conversations with strangers, or wait for them to start?
Would a conversation like that be likely to happen to you again?

part3.q: Why do people seem to find it easy to talk to strangers in some places — a train, a queue, a wedding — and almost impossible in others?
followups: What is it about those situations that gives people permission?
Is it the place, or the fact that you'll probably never meet again?

part3.q: In your country, is chatting to a stranger seen as friendly, or slightly suspicious?
followups: Does that depend on who is doing the talking — their age, their gender?
Has that attitude changed within your lifetime?

part3.q: Some cultures treat small talk as basic politeness; others find it empty and even dishonest. What do you think small talk is actually for?
followups: Could a society function without it?
Why do you think some people are so bad at it?

part3.q: People in big cities walk past thousands of strangers a day and speak to none of them. Is that anonymity a problem, or is it exactly what makes city life bearable?
followups: Would city life work if everyone greeted everyone?
Does that anonymity affect how people treat each other?

part3.q: Children are taught never to talk to strangers, and adults are encouraged to network with them. When should that switch happen, and does the early warning leave a mark?
followups: Do you think that childhood rule makes adults more hesitant?
How else could we teach children to be careful?

part3.q: Technology was supposed to connect people, yet many use headphones and screens precisely to avoid unplanned conversations. Has technology reduced our chance encounters?
followups: Are the connections apps create a fair replacement?
Is avoiding strangers a choice people are entitled to make?

part3.q: We routinely get into strangers' cars and sleep in strangers' homes through apps. Has technology actually increased trust between strangers, or just outsourced it to a rating system?
followups: What's the difference between trusting a person and trusting a platform?
Could that kind of system-based trust ever go badly wrong?

part3.q: Some researchers claim brief conversations with strangers make people measurably happier, yet almost everyone avoids them. Why would we systematically avoid something that's good for us?
followups: What are people actually afraid will happen?
Is that fear realistic, in your experience?

part3.q: Levels of social trust — how far people feel strangers can be trusted — differ enormously between countries. What do you think builds that kind of trust in a society, and what destroys it?
followups: Can a government do anything about it, or does it only grow from the bottom up?
How quickly can that trust be lost?

part3.q: If people increasingly live, work and shop without ever needing to speak to a stranger, what happens to a society over a generation or two?
followups: Is there a skill being lost, or just a habit?
Would anything realistically reverse that trend?

fc: Tells the Part 2 story with momentum — how it started, what was said, why it stuck — without circling back or restarting sentences.
Reconstructs dialogue smoothly ("so she asked me why I was carrying a telescope, and I ended up explaining…") — reported speech without losing the thread.
In Part 3, takes on genuinely hard questions (trust, anonymity) at a steady pace instead of speeding up nervously or grinding to a halt.
Uses natural hesitation devices when thinking ("Honestly, I've never been asked that — my instinct is…") rather than dead air.
Connects answers to each other: the point about headphones in one answer gets picked up when the rating-system question arrives.
lr: Precise topic language: strike up a conversation, break the ice, keep to yourself, a passing acquaintance, common ground, guard down.
Distinguishes near-synonyms cleanly: stranger vs outsider vs foreigner — mixing these up matters on exactly this topic.
Abstract Part 3 vocabulary handled naturally: anonymity, social fabric, vulnerability, etiquette, accountability, at face value.
Idioms placed sparingly and correctly: "we just clicked", "it broke the ice" — one apt idiom per section, not a shower of them.
Paraphrases 'talk to strangers' many ways across the test: approach someone, strike up a chat, engage with people you don't know, make small talk.
gra: Past narrative machinery in Part 2: "I'd been waiting for about an hour when the man next to me asked…" — past perfect and continuous doing real work.
Speculation about people in general: "people tend to…", "most of us would rather…", "there must be something about trains that…".
Conditionals for the sociological questions: "If everyone greeted everyone in Mumbai, nobody would get anywhere."
Contrast structures: "Whereas in a village everyone knows your business, in a city nobody knows your name — and both cut both ways."
Complex noun phrases without collapse: "the kind of trust that lets you fall asleep on a train full of people you've never met".
pron: Two voices in Part 2 — your narration and the stranger's reported words — separated by subtle shifts in tone, which is high-level delivery.
Stress lands on the operative contrasts: "we trust the platform, not the person".
Question-like intonation used deliberately when wondering aloud ("and maybe that's the point?") — variety that sounds thought, not read.
Connected speech in high-frequency chunks: "sort of", "you know what I mean", "never met them before" flow as single units.
Polysyllabic abstractions — anonymity, spontaneous, vulnerability, acquaintance — stressed correctly even mid-argument.

band9.part1: Give a direct answer, then one line of texture. For "Have you ever deleted an app because it was taking up too much of your time?" a Band 9 answer owns a specific case: "Yes — a short-video app, last year. I kept telling myself it was ten minutes and the clock kept saying forty, so it went." A named habit, a tiny number, a decision — that's what real answers are made of; nobody credible claims their phone use is perfectly disciplined.
part2: Set the scene fast — where you were, why you were there, and one visual detail (the delayed train, the rain, the empty waiting room) so the stranger enters a real place.
Show the opening move — who spoke first and the actual first line if you remember it; the mechanics of how strangers start talking is exactly what this card wants.
Compress the middle — pick the two or three turns the conversation took rather than replaying all of it; "we went from cricket to his years in the merchant navy" covers ground quickly.
Mark the shift — the moment it stopped being small talk: the surprising confession, the shared coincidence, the advice you didn't ask for but needed.
Answer the time bullet honestly — twenty minutes or four hours, and one clause on how it felt ("it went in a blink") to keep it a story, not a log.

Close on the residue — why it stayed with you and whether it changed your behaviour toward strangers; a small admission ("I still look for a seat next to someone interesting") lands the explain-clause.

part3.method: Answer → Explain → Example → Alternative View → Evaluation
part3.question: We routinely get into strangers' cars and sleep in strangers' homes through apps. Has technology actually increased trust between strangers, or just outsourced it to a rating system?
framework: Answer: commit to the sharper reading — e.g. it's mostly outsourcing: we haven't learned to trust strangers, we've learned to trust the score attached to them.

Explain: unpack the mechanism — the platform absorbs the risk assessment we used to do ourselves; the driver is a 4.9, so no judgement of the human is required, and the skill of reading people atrophies.

Example: make it concrete — you'll get into an unknown driver's car at midnight because an app says so, but might hesitate to accept a lift from a neighbour of ten years; the trust follows the interface, not the person.

Alternative view: concede what's real — repeated safe experiences do generalise; a generation that has couch-surfed across Europe is demonstrably more comfortable with strangers than their parents, whatever the mechanism.
Evaluate: land it — call it borrowed trust: it works brilliantly until the system fails, and a society should notice when its confidence in strangers can be switched off by a server outage.

mistakes.title: Describing a friend, not a stranger
mistakes.detail: Candidates reach for their best conversation story, which is usually with someone they knew. The card's engine is unfamiliarity — the not-knowing is what makes it memorable. If the person was already a friend, the story misses the point of every bullet.

mistakes.title: No actual conversation in the conversation story
mistakes.detail: "We talked about many things and it was very nice" gives the examiner nothing. One line of reported speech — what they asked, what you answered — is the difference between a story and a summary.

mistakes.title: Inventing a cinematic encounter
mistakes.detail: A suspiciously perfect stranger who delivers life-changing wisdom on a mountaintop sounds scripted, and scripted delivery follows. A real, modest encounter — the aunty on the bus who talked for an hour — is easier to speak about naturally and scores better.

mistakes.title: Turning Part 3 into a stranger-danger lecture
mistakes.detail: The questions probe trust, culture and cities. Answering each one with warnings about crime and being careful flattens ten different questions into one repeated safety announcement.

mistakes.title: Claiming your country for one answer and contradicting it the next
mistakes.detail: Saying people in your country never talk to strangers, then describing constant train-compartment friendships two answers later, signals answers assembled from stock phrases rather than thought. Keep your own picture consistent.

mistakes.title: The word 'strangers' on every fifth word
mistakes.detail: The topic traps you into repetition. Rotate: people you don't know, a passer-by, a fellow passenger, someone new, an unfamiliar face. Range here is cheap and visible.

mistakes.title: Answering the happiness-research question with 'yes, agreed'
mistakes.detail: That question hands you a paradox — we avoid what's good for us — and asks you to explain it. Agreeing with the research and stopping is a Band 6 move; the marks are in the why: fear of rejection, scripts we lack, energy costs.

mistakes.title: Treating the anonymity question as obviously bad
mistakes.detail: "Cities are cold and villages are warm" is a cliché the question explicitly challenges — it offers anonymity as possibly what makes city life bearable. Engaging with that provocation, even to reject it, shows the flexibility Band 8–9 needs.

mistakes.title: Vague app answers in Part 1
mistakes.detail: "I use social media and messaging apps" describes every phone on Earth. Name the app, name the habit — the examiner is scoring the specificity of your language, not the sophistication of your phone.

mistakes.title: Rushing the trust questions
mistakes.detail: The later Part 3 questions are the hardest in the test, and nervous candidates sprint through them in half-sentences. A slower, structured answer to one hard question outscores three breathless generalisations.
